reasoning_traces.think:
The core failure mode is that move sequence models must reconstruct the board state from scratch each turn (T) while also selecting high-quality moves (Q). These goals are antagonistic: low-rated games provide diverse board positions for tracking but offer weak move signals; high-rated games provide strong move signals but fewer distinct positions. Standard filtering discards the diversity, breaking T, while scaling increases model capacity but does not resolve the fundamental conflict. Elo weighting decouples the two objectives by adjusting the gradient flow: it amplifies the quality signal Q without destroying the diversity supply T. The resulting bottleneck P ≤ min(T, Q) predicts that performance will always be limited by the weaker capability, explaining why filtering hurts even though it reduces noise. The weighting sweet spot balances these competing demands, preventing Q from overwhelming T and causing catastrophic forgetting of earlier game states.

reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: This work builds on the theory of catastrophic forgetting in continual learning [Kirkpatrick et al., 2017] and the double descent phenomenon [Belkin et al., 2019]. It also draws inspiration from curriculum learning [Bengio et al., 2009], which schedules training difficulty, but applies it to a different axis: quality versus diversity. The dual-capability framework can be viewed as a form of multi-objective optimization where the Pareto frontier is collapsed into a hard bottleneck.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Opponents (humans or other engines) exploit weaknesses in either T or Q: a strong opponent can force a tracking failure by reaching rare positions, while a patient opponent can expose poor decision-making in familiar structures. A human-like engine must maintain a balance that makes its mistakes predictable yet avoidable, unlike superhuman engines whose errors are often statistically improbable. reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: The bottleneck P ≤ min(T, Q) would break if tracking and decision-making were completely independent tasks, e.g., if a separate world-model provided perfect board states to a decision policy. However, the authors show that filtering low-rated data still degrades performance, indicating that the two capabilities are tightly coupled during training from raw sequences. This coupling ensures that any mitigation strategy must affect both T and Q simultaneously, ruling out simple architectural separations.
